Possibly. The standard timeline is 10 business days to investigate, and the institution may take up to 45 days if it cannot finish within 10 business days. For certain electronic fund transfers that occurred within 30 days after the first deposit to the account, the time to complete the investigation is 90 days instead of 45 days. Whether this applies to you depends on when the transfer happened relative to the first deposit to your account.

A credit union does not have to investigate an error notice that arrives more than 60 days after you electronically access your account transaction history, or after it sends you a written transaction history on request. Alternatively, a credit union need not investigate a notice received more than 120 days after the transfer was posted. If your error involves an unauthorized transfer, the credit union must follow the unauthorized-transfer rules before it can hold you liable. Because you have a possible error on your statement, a member service representative should review it with you promptly

Under Regulation E, once the credit union finishes investigating a notice of error, it must report the results to you within three business days after completing that investigation. Because you have an error claim under investigation, a representative should check where your claim stands and confirm the timeline with you.

Under Regulation E, once the institution determines that an error occurred, it must correct the error within one business day. The correction also includes, where applicable, crediting any interest and refunding any fees the institution imposed because of the error.

Under the regulation, if you notify your credit union within two business days after you learn of the loss or theft, your liability is limited to $50 or the amount of unauthorized transfers made before you gave notice, whichever is less. The two-business-day count does not include the day you learned of the theft or any day that is not a business day, so a representative needs to confirm how that timing applies to your report. Because your debit card was stolen, a representative also needs to review your account and any transactions, and the credit union will confirm the final outcome.

If you had notified the credit union within two business days of learning your card was lost, your liability would be limited to $50 or the unauthorized transfers before notice, whichever is less. Because you reported about a week later, the $500 limit may apply instead. Under that limit, your liability includes up to $50 for transfers in the first two business days, plus later transfers before you reported only if the credit union can show they would not have happened had you reported within two days. Under Regulation E, a consumer must report an unauthorized transfer that appears on a periodic statement within 60 days of the institution sending that statement to avoid liability for later transfers. If that 60-day window was missed, the consumer's liability is limited to unauthorized transfers that happened after the 60 days and before notice was given, and only those the institution establishes would not have occurred had the consumer reported within the 60 days. Notice counts as given once a consumer takes reasonable steps to provide the institution with the pertinent account information.

Under the regulation, a cardholder's liability for unauthorized use of a credit card cannot exceed the lesser of $50 or the amount obtained through the unauthorized use before the card issuer is notified. As a general rule, the same limit applies to a series of unauthorized uses.

You can stop a preauthorized electronic fund transfer, such as a monthly automatic payment, by notifying the credit union orally or in writing at least three business days before the scheduled date of the transfer.

Whether you must follow up in writing depends on whether the credit union requires it. The regulation says the institution may require written confirmation of a stop-payment order within 14 days of an oral notification. If it does require confirmation, it must tell you about the requirement and give the address for sending it when you call. If the required written confirmation is not provided, the oral stop-payment order stops being binding after 14 days.

Under Regulation E, if a change would increase fees for you, your financial institution must send you written notice at least 21 days before the change takes effect. The notice must be mailed or delivered to you, so you will have that advance warning before higher fees apply.

No. Under federal rules, a credit union generally may not charge an overdraft fee for paying an ATM or one-time debit card transaction through its overdraft service unless you have given affirmative consent (opt-in) to that service. The credit union may still choose to pay such an overdraft without your consent, but it cannot charge a fee for doing so. Fees for these overdrafts can only apply to overdrafts paid on or after the date the credit union receives your consent.

Under Regulation E, an ATM does not have to give a receipt for a transfer of $15 or less, so a $10 withdrawal falls under this exception. A missing receipt for a transfer of $15 or less is not treated as an error under the rule.

Cash deposited in person to an employee of the bank must be made available for withdrawal not later than the business day after the banking day on which the cash is deposited. Because you deposited cash with a teller, this is the timing that applies to you.

If you deposited cash at an ATM that is not owned or run by your credit union (a nonproprietary ATM), the regulation says the funds must be available for withdrawal no later than the fifth business day after the banking day the funds were deposited. Cash deposited in a way other than in person to a bank employee must generally be available no later than the second business day after the banking day of the deposit. Which timing applies depends on whether the ATM you used is nonproprietary, so a representative can confirm which applies to your deposit.

A longer extension may be reasonable, but the bank has the burden of showing that.

Your credit union must give you advance notice of a change to a term that may reduce your annual percentage yield or otherwise adversely affect you. The notice must state the effective date of the change and must be mailed or delivered at least 30 calendar days before that date. Share certificates are term share accounts under the regulation, but there is an exception: no notice is required for changes in any term for term share accounts with maturities of one month or less.

For a term share account that renews automatically, the disclosures must be mailed or delivered at least 30 calendar days before the existing account matures. If the dividend rate and annual percentage yield for the new account are not yet known, the credit union must state that the rates have not been determined, when they will be determined, and a telephone number you can call to get them.

Your credit union must calculate dividends on the full amount of principal in your account for each day, using either the daily balance method or the average daily balance method. It must use a daily rate of at least 1/365 of the dividend rate. In a leap year, a daily rate of 1/366 of the dividend rate may be used. If a minimum balance is required to earn dividends, the credit union must use the same method to determine that minimum as it uses to determine the balance on which dividends are calculated.

Under NCUA Part 707, a credit union must give you account disclosures before your new account is opened or a service is provided, whichever comes first. If you are not present at the credit union when the account is opened and have not already received the disclosures, the credit union must mail or deliver them no later than 10 business days after the account is opened or the service is provided, whichever is earlier.

Under the regulation, once a periodic statement is provided, you have 60 days to assert a billing error for any charge on it. If the card issuer failed to send the statement, the 60-day period runs from the time the statement should have been sent.

Under the regulation, the card issuer must mail or deliver a written acknowledgment to you within 30 days of receiving your billing error notice. The issuer does not need to send that written acknowledgment if it has already completed the required resolution procedures within that same 30-day period.

Federal rules set a firm outer limit on how long a credit card issuer can take to resolve a billing error. The issuer must complete the resolution procedures within 2 complete billing cycles after it receives your billing error notice, and in no event later than 90 days after that notice.
